data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible without smuggling in induction if reinterpreted as a non-epistemic, methodological rule of 'critical selection' rather than an expectation of future success; however, accepting this defense costs the scientist any rational assurance that the chosen theory will work in practice, reducing scientific action to a blind evolutionary gamble.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the Tich\u00fd/Miller proof holds that verisimilitude cannot be estimated, then the 'better' in 'better-corroborated' loses its normative force for truth-likeness.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory (e.g., building a bridge) inherently requires an assumption of its reliability, then merely labeling the preference 'methodological' is a semantic evasion of the pragmatic need for induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's own advice to 'act on the best tested theory' implies an expectation of success, then his practice contradicts his strict prohibition against inductive inference.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'corroboration' (a logical report of past performance) and 'prediction' (an inductive leap). Popper's preference is framed not as believing Theory A is more likely true than Theory B, but as a procedural commitment to test the most vulnerable (high content) theory that has so far survived. The preference is a rule of the game of science, akin to a chess player preferring a gambit that has worked before, not because it guarantees a win, but because it offers the fastest route to checkmate or refutation. This avoids induction by refusing to assign higher probability to the future success of the gambit.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
